name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0901 - Modulus of rigidity of ideal liquids

questiontext.text: Modulus of rigidity of ideal liquids is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Modulus of rigidity (shear modulus, \(\eta\)) is defined as the ratio of tangential (shearing) stress to shearing strain: \(\eta = \frac{\text{Shearing stress}}{\text{Shearing strain}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation and Application
An ideal liquid has zero viscosity and offers no resistance to tangential or shearing forces. Consequently, it cannot sustain any shearing stress in equilibrium, meaning the shearing stress is zero for any shear deformation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Since the shearing stress is zero, the modulus of rigidity of an ideal liquid is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0902 - Maximum load a wire can withstand when length halved

questiontext.text: The maximum load a wire can withstand without breaking, when its length is reduced to half of its original length, will

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The breaking stress (ultimate tensile strength) of a wire is an intensive property that depends only on the material of the wire and temperature, not on its dimensions.

Step 2: Evaluation and Application
The maximum load (breaking force) a wire can withstand is given by \(F_{\text{max}} = \text{Breaking stress} \times A\), where \(A\) is the cross-sectional area of the wire. Neither the breaking stress nor the cross-sectional area depends on the length of the wire.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
When the length of the wire is reduced to half of its original length, the maximum load it can withstand without breaking will remain the same.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0903 - Effect of doubling temperature on Youngs modulus

questiontext.text: The temperature of a wire is doubled. The Young's modulus of elasticity

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elasticity of a solid arises from the restoring interatomic forces between its constituent atoms. Young's modulus of elasticity is directly proportional to the strength of these interatomic binding forces.

Step 2: Evaluation and Application
When the temperature of a wire is increased (doubled), the thermal agitation of the atoms increases and the average interatomic separation increases due to thermal expansion. This weakens the interatomic restoring forces, making the material easier to deform under a given stress.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the interatomic forces weaken with rising temperature, the Young's modulus of elasticity of the wire will decrease.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0904 - Strain produced in a stretched spring

questiontext.text: A spring is stretched by applying a load to its free end. The strain produced in the spring is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Longitudinal strain is associated with a change in length along the axis of loading, whereas shear strain is associated with a change in shape or twisting of the cross-section of a wire.

Step 2: Evaluation and Application
When a helical spring is stretched by applying an axial load at its free end, the overall length of the spring increases, producing longitudinal strain. At the same time, the wire forming the coils of the spring undergoes twisting (torsion), which produces shear strain in the material of the wire.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the strain produced in a stretched spring is both longitudinal and shear.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0905 - Ratio of diameters of copper and iron wires

questiontext.text: A rigid bar of mass \(M\) is supported symmetrically by three wires each of length \(l\). Those at each end are of copper and the middle one is of iron. The ratio of their diameters, if each is to have the same tension, is equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the rigid bar \(= M\). Three vertical wires each of length \(l\) support the bar symmetrically: two outer wires of copper (Young's modulus \(Y_{\text{copper}}\)) and one middle wire of iron (Young's modulus \(Y_{\text{iron}}\)). Each wire has the same tension \(T\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because the bar is rigid and supported symmetrically, it remains horizontal, so all three wires undergo the same elongation \(\Delta l\) and hence the same longitudinal strain \(\frac{\Delta l}{l}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Young's modulus is given by:
\[Y = \frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} = \frac{T / A}{\Delta l / l}\]
where the cross-sectional area of a wire of diameter \(d\) is \(A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Rearranging the Young's modulus formula for the area \(A\):
\[A = \frac{T l}{Y \Delta l}\]
Substituting \(A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}\):
\[\frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{T l}{Y \Delta l}\]
Since \(T\), \(l\), and \(\Delta l\) are identical for all three wires, \(d^2 \propto \frac{1}{Y}\), or \(d \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{Y}}\).
Taking the ratio of the diameter of the copper wire to that of the iron wire:
\[\frac{d_{\text{copper}}}{d_{\text{iron}}} = \sqrt{\frac{Y_{\text{iron}}}{Y_{\text{copper}}}}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ratio is dimensionless, as required for a ratio of diameters. Since copper has a smaller Young's modulus than iron, the copper wire needs a larger diameter to carry the same tension at the same strain. Thus, the ratio of their diameters is \(\sqrt{\frac{Y_{\text{iron}}}{Y_{\text{copper}}}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0906 - Strain in a wire stretched horizontally between pillars

questiontext.text: A mild steel wire of length \(2L\) and cross-sectional area \(A\) is stretched, well within elastic limit, horizontally between two pillars (Fig. 9.1). A mass \(m\) is suspended from the mid point of the wire. Strain in the wire is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Original length of the wire \(= 2L\), cross-sectional area \(= A\). A mass \(m\) suspended at the midpoint depresses the midpoint vertically downward by a distance \(x\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Since the deformation is well within the elastic limit of mild steel, the depression is small compared to the half-length, i.e., \(x \ll L\). Each half of the wire forms the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with horizontal base \(L\) and vertical side \(x\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Longitudinal strain is defined as:
\[\text{Strain} = \frac{\Delta l}{l_0}\]
where \(\Delta l\) is the change in length and \(l_0 = 2L\) is the original length. For \(u \ll 1\), the binomial approximation gives \((1 + u)^{1/2} \approx 1 + \frac{u}{2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The stretched length of each half of the wire is:
\[L' = \sqrt{L^2 + x^2} = L \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{L^2}\right)^{1/2}\]
Applying the binomial approximation for \(x \ll L\):
\[L' \approx L \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{2L^2}\right) = L + \frac{x^2}{2L}\]
The total stretched length of the wire is \(2L' = 2L + \frac{x^2}{L}\).
Hence, the increase in length is:
\[\Delta l = 2L' - 2L = \frac{x^2}{L}\]
Dividing by the original length \(2L\) gives the strain:
\text{Strain} = \frac{\Delta l}{2L} = \frac{x^2 / L}{2L} = \frac{x^2}{2L^2}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The expression \(\frac{x^2}{2L^2}\) is dimensionless and positive, and it vanishes when \(x = 0\), as expected. Therefore, the strain in the wire is \(\frac{x^2}{2L^2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0907 - Tension in strings suspending a rectangular frame

questiontext.text:
A rectangular frame is to be suspended symmetrically by two strings of equal length on two supports (Fig. 9.2). It can be done in one of the following three ways;

The tension in the strings will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A rectangular frame of weight \(mg\) is suspended symmetrically by two strings of equal length in three configurations: strings inclined outward, strings vertical, and strings inclined inward.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let \(\theta\) be the angle that each string makes with the vertical, and \(T\) be the tension in each string (equal by symmetry). Upward forces are taken as positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For static vertical equilibrium of the frame, the sum of the vertical components of tension must balance the weight:
\[2T \cos\theta = mg \implies T = \frac{mg}{2\cos\theta}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
When the two strings are vertical, \(\theta = 0^\circ\), so \(\cos\theta = \cos 0^\circ = 1\), which is the maximum possible value of \(\cos\theta\). This gives the minimum tension:
\[T_{\text{min}} = \frac{mg}{2}\]
When the strings are inclined outward or inward, \(\theta > 0^\circ\), so \(\cos\theta < 1\), which makes \(T > \frac{mg}{2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
As \(\theta\) increases from \(0^\circ\), \(\cos\theta\) decreases and tension \(T\) increases. Therefore, the tension in the strings is least in the vertical suspension configuration, which corresponds to configuration (b).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0908 - Elongation and shape change of rubber and steel rods

questiontext.text: Consider two cylindrical rods of identical dimensions, one of rubber and the other of steel. Both the rods are fixed rigidly at one end to the roof. A mass \(M\) is attached to each of the free ends at the centre of the rods.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The elongation and local deformation of a rod under a central point load depend on its Young's modulus \(Y\) and shear rigidity. A material with a very high Young's modulus resists both stretching and local shear deformation, whereas a material with a very low Young's modulus deforms appreciably.

Step 2: Evaluation and Application
Steel has a very large Young's modulus (\(Y \approx 2 \times 10^{11}\text{ N m}^{-2}\)), so under the weight \(Mg\) attached at the centre of its free end, it elongates slightly without any perceptible change in the shape of its bottom face. In contrast, rubber has a very small Young's modulus. Because the mass \(M\) is attached at the centre of the free end, the central region experiences greater downward pull and stretches much more than the outer edges, causing the bottom edge of the rubber rod to taper to a tip at the centre.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The steel rod will elongate without any perceptible change in shape, while the rubber rod will elongate with the shape of the bottom edge tapered to a tip at the centre.

answer.text: Both the rods will elongate but there shall be no perceptible change in shape.
The steel rod will elongate and change shape but the rubber rod will only elongate.
The steel rod will elongate without any perceptible change in shape, but the rubber rod will elongate and the shape of the bottom edge will change to an ellipse.
The steel rod will elongate, without any perceptible change in shape, but the rubber rod will elongate with the shape of the bottom edge tapered to a tip at the centre.

questiontext.text: The stress-strain graphs for two materials are shown in Fig. 9.3 (assume same scale).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two stress-strain curves for Material (i) and Material (ii) are plotted on the same scale, showing the linear limit, ultimate tension strength, and fracture point for each.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The elastic region is the region up to the linear (proportional) limit on the strain axis. Brittleness is indicated by how close the fracture point is to the ultimate tension strength (a small plastic region between ultimate tension strength and fracture point indicates greater brittleness).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Young's modulus \(Y\) is the slope of the linear portion of the stress-strain graph. A material with a larger linear strain range is elastic over a larger region of strain, while a material with a smaller plastic deformation range before fracture is more brittle.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the two graphs:
1. The linear limit in Material (ii) extends to a larger value of strain than in Material (i), so Material (ii) is elastic over a larger region of strain compared to Material (i).
2. In Material (ii), the fracture point lies very close to the ultimate tension strength, leaving a much smaller plastic region than in Material (i). Hence, Material (ii) is more brittle than Material (i).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both conclusions follow directly from the relative positions of the linear limit, ultimate tension strength, and fracture point on the two curves. Therefore, Material (ii) is elastic over a larger region of strain as compared to Material (i), and Material (ii) is more brittle than Material (i).

answer.text: Material (ii) is more elastic than material (i) and hence material (ii) is more brittle.
Material (i) and (ii) have the same elasticity and the same brittleness.
Material (ii) is elastic over a larger region of strain as compared to (i).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0910 - Tensile stress and tension in a suspended wire

questiontext.text: A wire is suspended from the ceiling and stretched under the action of a weight \(F\) suspended from its other end. The force exerted by the ceiling on it is equal and opposite to the weight.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A wire of cross-sectional area \(A\) is suspended vertically from a ceiling and pulled downward by a weight \(F\) at its lower end. The ceiling exerts an equal and opposite upward force \(F\) at the upper end.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The weight of the wire itself is negligible compared to the suspended weight \(F\), and the wire is in static equilibrium.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Tensile stress at any cross-section of area \(A\) is defined as the internal restoring force (tension \(T\)) acting perpendicular to the cross-section divided by the cross-sectional area:
\[\text{Tensile stress} = \frac{T}{A}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Consider any cross-section of the wire. For the lower portion of the wire below this cross-section to be in equilibrium under the downward weight \(F\), the upper portion must exert an upward internal force (tension) \(T = F\) at that cross-section.
Therefore, the tension at any cross-section of the wire is \(F\).
Dividing this tension by the cross-sectional area \(A\) gives the tensile stress at any cross-section:
\[\text{Tensile stress} = \frac{F}{A}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The tension is \(F\) (not \(2F\) or \(0\)), and the tensile stress has units of force per unit area, \(\frac{F}{A}\). Thus, both the tensile stress at any cross-section \(A\) of the wire is \(\frac{F}{A}\) and the tension at any cross-section \(A\) of the wire is \(F\).

answer.text: Tensile stress at any cross section \(A\) of the wire is \(F / A\).
Tensile stress at any cross section is zero.
Tensile stress at any cross section \(A\) of the wire is \(2F / A\).
Tension at any cross section \(A\) of the wire is \(F\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0911 - Rod suspended by steel and aluminium wires

questiontext.text:
A rod of length \(l\) and negligible mass is suspended at its two ends by two wires of steel (wire A) and aluminium (wire B) of equal lengths (Fig. 9.4). The cross-sectional areas of wires A and B are \(1.0\text{ mm}^2\) and \(2.0\text{ mm}^2\), respectively.

\[Y_{\text{Al}} = 70 \times 10^9\text{ Nm}^{-2} \text{ and } Y_{\text{steel}} = 200 \times 10^9\text{ Nm}^{-2}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of rod \(= l\) (negligible mass). Wire A (steel): \(A_A = 1.0\text{ mm}^2\), \(Y_A = 200 \times 10^9\text{ N m}^{-2}\). Wire B (aluminium): \(A_B = 2.0\text{ mm}^2\), \(Y_B = 70 \times 10^9\text{ N m}^{-2}\). Both wires have equal length.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let mass \(m\) be suspended at a distance \(x\) from wire A and \((l - x)\) from wire B. Let \(T_A\) and \(T_B\) be the tensions in wires A and B, respectively.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For rotational equilibrium about the point of suspension of mass \(m\):
\[T_A x = T_B (l - x) \implies \frac{x}{l - x} = \frac{T_B}{T_A}\]
Stress is \(\sigma = \frac{T}{A}\), and strain is \(\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{Y} = \frac{T}{A Y}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Case 1 (Equal stresses, \(\sigma_A = \sigma_B\)):
\[\frac{T_A}{A_A} = \frac{T_B}{A_B} \implies \frac{T_B}{T_A} = \frac{A_B}{A_A} = \frac{2.0}{1.0} = 2\]
Using rotational equilibrium:
\[\frac{x}{l - x} = 2 \implies x = \frac{2l}{3}\]
Since \(x = \frac{2l}{3} > \frac{l}{2}\), mass \(m\) is closer to wire B.

Case 2 (Equal strains, \(\varepsilon_A = \varepsilon_B\)):
\[\frac{T_A}{A_A Y_A} = \frac{T_B}{A_B Y_B} \implies \frac{T_B}{T_A} = \frac{A_B Y_B}{A_A Y_A} = \frac{2.0 \times 70 \times 10^9}{1.0 \times 200 \times 10^9} = \frac{140}{200} = 0.7\]
Using rotational equilibrium:
\[\frac{x}{l - x} = 0.7 \implies x = \frac{0.7}{1.7} l < \frac{l}{2}\]
Since \(x < \frac{l}{2}\), mass \(m\) is closer to wire A.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
For equal stresses, the thicker wire (wire B) must carry double the tension, placing \(m\) closer to B. For equal strains, the stiffer product \(AY\) belongs to wire A (\(200 > 140\)), so wire A must carry more tension, placing \(m\) closer to wire A. Thus, mass \(m\) should be suspended close to B for equal stresses, and close to wire A for equal strain.

answer.text: Mass \(m\) should be suspended close to wire A to have equal stresses in both the wires.
Mass \(m\) should be suspended close to B to have equal stresses in both the wires.
Mass \(m\) should be suspended at the middle of the wires to have equal stresses in both the wires.
Mass \(m\) should be suspended close to wire A to have equal strain in both wires.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0912 - Bulk modulus and shear modulus of an ideal liquid

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An ideal liquid is defined as one that is completely incompressible and has zero viscosity (cannot sustain any tangential or shearing stress). Bulk modulus is \(B = -V \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V}\), and shear modulus is \(\eta = \frac{\text{Shearing stress}}{\text{Shearing strain}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation and Application
1. Since an ideal liquid is incompressible, \(\Delta V = 0\) for any finite change in pressure \(\Delta P\), which makes the bulk modulus \(B = \infty\) (infinite).
2. Since an ideal liquid offers no resistance to tangential forces, it cannot sustain any shearing stress, which makes the shear modulus \(\eta = 0\) (zero).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
For an ideal liquid, the bulk modulus is infinite and the shear modulus is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_MECHANICALPROPERTIESOFSOLIDS_MCQ_Q0913 - Stress and strain in copper and steel wires in series

questiontext.text: A copper and a steel wire of the same diameter are connected end to end. A deforming force \(F\) is applied to this composite wire which causes a total elongation of \(1\text{ cm}\). The two wires will have

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A copper wire and a steel wire of the same diameter \(d\) (hence equal cross-sectional area \(A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}\)) are connected end to end (in series) and subjected to a deforming force \(F\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The wires are of negligible mass compared to the applied force \(F\), so the tension throughout the composite wire is uniform and equal to \(F\). The deformation is within the elastic limit of both materials.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Tensile stress is \(\sigma = \frac{F}{A}\).
By Hooke's law, longitudinal strain is \(\varepsilon = \frac{\sigma}{Y} = \frac{F}{A Y}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Since both wires carry the same tension \(F\) and have the same cross-sectional area \(A\), the tensile stress \(\sigma = \frac{F}{A}\) is identical in both wires.
2. Since Young's modulus of steel is greater than that of copper (\(Y_{\text{steel}} \neq Y_{\text{copper}}\)), the strains \(\varepsilon_{\text{copper}} = \frac{\sigma}{Y_{\text{copper}}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\text{steel}} = \frac{\sigma}{Y_{\text{steel}}}\) are different.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The two wires experience the same stress because \(F\) and \(A\) are identical, and they experience different strains because their Young's moduli are different.
